title: The Impacts of Environmental Regulations on Industrial Activity
research_question: How do federally mandated air pollution regulations affect the level of industrial activity—specifically employment, capital investment, and output—in polluting manufacturing industries? Do these regulations meaningfully retard the growth of regulated manufacturers in heavily polluted areas relative to cleaner ones?
data_description: The analysis combines two main data sources covering 1967–1987. Manufacturing data come from the plant-level microdata of the five quinquennial Censuses of Manufactures (1967, 1972, 1977, 1982, 1987), totaling about 1.75 million plant observations, with information on employment, capital stock, value of shipments, plant age, multi-unit firm status, 4-digit SIC industry, and county of location. A unique plant identifier permits longitudinal tracking. Regulatory data consist of annual, county-level, pollutant-specific attainment/nonattainment designations for carbon monoxide, ozone, sulfur dioxide, and total suspended particulates, hand-compiled for all 3,070 U.S. counties from the Code of Federal Regulations and, for early years, from EPA pollution monitor readings (Quick Look Report). EPA industry-emissions estimates are used to classify 12 manufacturing industries as emitters of one or more regulated pollutants. The unit of observation is a plant-by-five-year period.
institutional_context: The setting is the U.S. Clean Air Act, particularly the 1970 and 1977 Amendments, under which the EPA set national ambient air quality standards for four criteria pollutants (CO, ozone, SO2, TSPs). Each year, every U.S. county received separate attainment or nonattainment designations for each pollutant based on whether local concentrations exceeded the federal standard. In nonattainment counties, states were required to impose plant-specific controls on major emitters of the relevant pollutant—mandating state-of-the-art abatement equipment, emissions permits, and (after 1977) offsetting emission reductions for new investment—while existing plants faced binding emission limits. In attainment counties, requirements were considerably weaker, and non-emitting plants were unregulated in either category. The pollutant-specific designations changed over time as air quality evolved, and enforcement was backed by federal and state inspections and penalties, generating sharp differences in regulatory stringency across counties, industries, and years.
